raw_response:
I have worked this land for 45 years. My father farmed before me, and I know every corner of these 8.5 mu. Three of my children have gone to work in factories in Shijiazhuang and Baoding — good for them, but it means my wife and I manage most of the field work ourselves now, with help during busy seasons. My back is not what it was at 30, but I know what this land needs.

I will keep 6 mu in the wheat-maize rotation like always. This is the backbone. Wheat goes in the ground in October once I finish the maize harvest. I do rotary tillage — it breaks up the compacted soil well enough and does not take too long. I use the compound fertilizer bags from the village supply shop, the kind with nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium together for the base application, then I top-dress with urea before the grain fills out. I water three times: once before the ground freezes in winter to help the roots establish, once at jointing, and once at heading. Our well is deep but water costs money to pump, so I do not water more than I have to.

After the wheat comes off in June, I put maize straight into the same ground — no-till, direct seeding to save time and keep moisture in. Hybrid seeds from the county market have given me good results for years. Summer rains take care of some of the water needs, but if July or August runs dry I will pump two or three times. Maize needs heavy nitrogen — I put on more than some people recommend but I have seen what happens when you go light on it.

For cotton I keep 2.5 mu on the side. The price is not what it was ten or fifteen years ago, but I know cotton and my wife handles some of the topping and picking. The hard part is the insects — bollworms, aphids, spider mites. I spray seven or eight times across the season. My knees hurt carrying the sprayer but it has to be done. I plough that ground in spring before transplanting.
